sections.h: Jeremiah and the last kings (chapters 21-25)
sections.b: Chapters 21 to 25 follow Jeremiah from the siege of 588 BC back to the year the first scroll was written (605-604 BC). He answers Zedekiah's request for a wonder with the choice of life or death (21), judges the three sons and grandson of Josiah (22), promises a righteous Branch and condemns the prophets who promise peace (23), reads the exiles of 597 as good figs and the people left behind as bad ones (24), and sums up twenty-three years of unheeded warning, fixing seventy years for Babylon and handing the nations the cup of rage (25).

sections.h: Zedekiah in Jeremiah 21-25
sections.b: Zedekiah (Mattaniah), Josiah's son and Jehoiachin's uncle, ruled from 597 to 586 BC. He asks Jeremiah for a wonder during the siege and is told the LORD is fighting against the city (21:1-10). The name Nebuchadnezzar gave him, "my righteousness is the LORD," is turned around in the Branch's name "The LORD is our righteousness" (23:5-6). In the vision of the figs he and his officials are the bad figs (24:8-10).

sections.h: Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22 and 25
sections.b: Jehoiakim (Eliakim), made king by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC, reigned until 598. Jeremiah accuses him of building a cedar palace with unpaid labor and shedding innocent blood, and contrasts him with his father Josiah (22:13-19). The threat that he would be buried like a donkey is hard to match with Kings and Chronicles (22:19 note). The prophecy of 25:1-14 is dated to his fourth year, the same year as the burned scroll of chapter 36.

sections.h: Coniah's curse and what followed
sections.b: Jehoiachin is called Coniah in Jeremiah 22:24-30 and Jeconiah in 24:1. He reigned about three months, surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in March 597 BC and was taken to Babylon with the court. Jeremiah says he will be torn off like a signet ring and that none of his offspring will rule in Judah. The signet image is reversed in Haggai 2:23, and Matthew lists Jeconiah in the line of Jesus. Babylonian tablets name him "Ya'ukin, king of Judah" and five sons, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 records his release in 561 BC.

sections.h: The Branch in Jeremiah 23
sections.b: Jeremiah promises that the LORD will "raise up for David a righteous Branch" who will rule wisely, carry out justice and righteousness, and be called "The LORD is our righteousness" (23:5-6; repeated in 33:15-16). The Hebrew word tsemach is a sprout from a cut stump. The Greek translates it anatole, "dawn" (compare Luke 1:78). Zechariah uses "Branch" as a name (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12). Jewish tradition reads it as the Messiah (the Targum, Radak); Christians read it of Jesus.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 23:5-6; Jeremiah 33:15-16; Isaiah 11:1; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78

common: The Branch is a king of David's line whom the LORD will raise up after the failed kings.
uncommon: Some critics hold the oracle first meant a restored king in Zedekiah's or Zerubbabel's day.

sections.h: Josiah in the oracles on his sons
sections.b: Josiah is held up as the model king in Jeremiah 22: he "took up the case of the poor and the needy" and that is what "knowing me" means (22:15-16). His death at Megiddo in 609 BC is the grief people should leave behind for the greater grief of his son Shallum's exile (22:10-12). Jeremiah's twenty-three years of preaching begin in Josiah's thirteenth year (25:3).

sections.h: Shepherds who scatter, and a shepherd who gathers
sections.b: Jeremiah calls the rulers of Judah shepherds who have lost and scattered the flock (23:1-2), promises that the LORD will gather the remnant from all the lands and set new shepherds over them (23:3-4), and at the end of chapter 25 tells the shepherds of every nation to howl (25:34-36). The image runs from the "wind" that will shepherd Judah's rulers (22:22) to Ezekiel 34 and John 10.

sections.h: The Branch and the signet ring
sections.b: Jeremiah 22:24-30 and 23:5-6 stand side by side: the last king's line is cut off, and the LORD promises to raise up a righteous Branch. The curse on Jehoiachin shapes the debate on Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:11-12; Luke 3). The Targum reads the Branch as a Messiah of the righteous, and Radak calls the Branch the Messiah; Christians see Jesus.

sections.h: David's throne at stake in Jeremiah
sections.b: Jeremiah sets the promise to David under conditions: if the royal house carries out justice, kings will keep passing through the palace gates; if not, the house becomes a ruin (22:1-5). Jehoiachin's line is cut off from the throne (22:30), yet the LORD will raise a righteous Branch for David (23:5-6). Haggai 2:23 turns the signet-ring image toward David's line again.

sections.h: Test the prophet: Jeremiah 23
sections.b: Jeremiah 23:9-40 is one of the fullest treatments of false prophets in the Old Testament. The marks of a false prophet are that he speaks from his own heart and not the mouth of the LORD (23:16), has not stood in the LORD's council (23:18), promises peace to the unrepentant (23:17), steals words from other prophets (23:30), and does the people no good (23:32). The test is the source, the message and the effect of the word.

sections.h: What a prophet is, in Jeremiah 23
sections.b: A true prophet has "taken a stand in the council of the LORD" and heard his word (23:18, 22). The prophets Jeremiah opposed also claimed dreams and used the formula "the LORD declares" (23:25, 31). The chapter holds that prophecy is not defined by a claim of inspiration but by what is said and what it does to the hearers.

sections.h: The council the prophet must stand in
sections.b: Jeremiah 23:18 and 23:22 describe the true prophet as one who has stood in the LORD's council (sod), the heavenly court where the LORD decides, and has heard his word there. The false prophets have not. The same picture appears in 1 Kings 22:19-23, Isaiah 6 and Amos 3:7.

sections.h: Dreams in Jeremiah 23
sections.b: The prophets Jeremiah attacks say, "I had a dream! I had a dream!" (23:25). Dreams are not condemned: the prophet who has a dream may tell it (23:28). What Jeremiah rejects is dreams presented as the word of the LORD, which make the people forget his name as the Baal worship once did (23:27).

sections.h: The prophets of Baal in Samaria
sections.b: Jeremiah says Samaria's prophets "prophesied by Baal and made my people Israel wander" (23:13) and that the Jerusalem prophets' dreams make the people forget the LORD's name "for Baal" as their ancestors did (23:27). Jerusalem's prophets, who speak in the LORD's name, are named worse than Samaria's.

sections.h: Jerusalem's prophets are Sodom
sections.b: Jeremiah 23:14 says that to the LORD all of Jerusalem's prophets are like Sodom and the city's people like Gomorrah, because they live by lies and strengthen the wicked so that no one turns back. The comparison is with Sodom's persistence in sin, not with a specific act.

sections.h: Wormwood in Jeremiah 23
sections.b: The LORD says he will feed the false prophets wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, because pollution has gone out from them to the whole land (23:15). The same "food" is promised to the people at 9:15 and recalls the bitter root of Deuteronomy 29:18.

sections.h: The word as fire and hammer
sections.b: "Is my word not like fire... and like a hammer that smashes rock?" (23:29). The prophet's word is not a dream or a private opinion. The rabbis read the hammer as a picture of the many meanings in one verse (Bavli Sanhedrin 34a), and Hebrews 4:12 calls the word of God living and sharper than a two-edged sword.

sections.h: The remnant gathered from all the lands
sections.b: In 23:3 the LORD promises to gather "what is left of my flock" from every land where he drove them, and in 23:7-8 the return from the north is set above the Exodus as the oath formula of the future. Chapter 24 names the exiles of 597 as the good figs, and the people left in Jerusalem and Egypt as bad ones.

sections.h: The good figs and the bad figs
sections.b: Jeremiah 24 reverses what the people in Jerusalem thought: the exiles of 597 BC are the good figs, whom the LORD will watch over, bring back, build up and plant, while Zedekiah, his officials, the people still in the land and those who fled to Egypt are the figs too bad to eat. The new heart in 24:7 prepares for the new covenant.

sections.h: A heart to know me, and the covenant formula
sections.b: In 24:7 the LORD promises the exiles "a heart to know me" and says, "They will become my people, and I will become their God," the covenant formula that Jeremiah repeats at 31:33 and 32:38. The sin that ended the old covenant is named in 22:9: "they abandoned the covenant of the LORD their God."

sections.h: Seventy years in Jeremiah 25
sections.b: Jeremiah 25:11-12 says "these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years," and that when the seventy years are over the LORD will punish Babylon. The Greek says the people will serve "among the nations" and does not name Babylon. Chronicles reads the span as the land's sabbath rest (2 Chronicles 36:21), Zechariah counts from the temple's fall to its rebuilding, and Daniel 9 reinterprets it as seventy weeks of years.

sections.h: Babylon drinks last
sections.b: Babylon is first called the LORD's tool and then promised its own punishment: Nebuchadnezzar is "my servant" (25:9), the nations will serve Babylon seventy years (25:11), and when they are over the LORD will punish its king (25:12). In the cup passage the king of Sheshach, which is Babylon in the atbash cipher, drinks after all the others (25:26).

sections.h: Nebuchadnezzar in Jeremiah 21-25
sections.b: Nebuchadnezzar appears as the king whose army besieges Jerusalem (21:2), as the one who will burn the city (21:7, 10), as the king who took Jeconiah into exile (24:1) and as "my servant" whom the LORD sends against Judah (25:9). The synchronism in 25:1 puts his first year in Jehoiakim's fourth, 605-604 BC.

sections.h: The cup of the wine of rage
sections.b: Jeremiah is told to take from the LORD's hand a cup of the wine of rage and make the nations drink it, from Jerusalem to Babylon, until they stagger, vomit and fall (25:15-29). The image runs through Isaiah 51:17-22, Psalm 75:8, Habakkuk 2:15-16, Ezekiel 23:31-34 and Revelation 14:10.

sections.h: The cup list and the start of the nation oracles
sections.b: Jeremiah 25:15-26 lists the nations that will drink the cup: Jerusalem, Egypt, the mixed peoples, Uz, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, the coastlands, Dedan, Tema, Buz, Arabia, Zimri, Elam, Media, the northern kings and Sheshach (Babylon). The Hebrew puts the nation oracles in chapters 46 to 51; the Greek places them right after 25:13.

sections.h: The Greek and Hebrew texts of Jeremiah 23 and 25
sections.b: Jeremiah 23 and 25 show the two editions clearly. The Greek lacks 23:30-31, a clause in 23:36, 25:14 and 25:26's Sheshach; it reads "Josedek" for the Branch's name in 23:6; it places the oracles against the nations after 25:13. 4QJer-c shows the longer Hebrew text in part at 25:7, at "Zimri" in 25:25 and at Sheshach in 25:26 (its other words in 25:24-25 are restored). Tov and Bogaert hold that the Greek translates an earlier edition.

sections.h: Justice as knowing the LORD
sections.b: In Jeremiah 22 the king's first duty is to give justice to the poor: "Each morning, give a true verdict" (21:12; 22:3). Josiah "took up the case of the poor and the needy" and "Is this not knowing me?" (22:15-16). Jehoiakim's palace, built with unpaid labor, is the opposite.

sections.h: The last kings of Judah
sections.b: Chapters 21 to 23 are a book about the end of the Davidic monarchy in Jeremiah's time: the failing Zedekiah (21), the three sons of Josiah and grandson (22) and the promise of a Branch (23). Kingship is judged by justice for the poor, not by buildings.

sections.h: The LORD fights against Judah
sections.b: In 21:4-5 the LORD turns the defenders' weapons around and fights against Jerusalem "with a hand stretched out and a strong arm," the Exodus formula turned on Israel. He "sets apart" destroyers against the palace (22:7), and puts Judah and its neighbors under the ban (25:9).

sections.h: The way of life and the way of death
sections.b: Jeremiah offers the besieged people of Jerusalem a way of life, to go out to the Chaldeans, and a way of death, to stay (21:8-9). The choice repeats Deuteronomy 30:15-19, and the Didache opens with the same pair of ways.

sections.h: "The LORD is our righteousness"
sections.b: Jeremiah 23:6 gives the Branch the name "The LORD is our righteousness." Reformation debates on justification turned partly on this verse: whether Christ's righteousness is counted as the believer's or made inwardly the believer's. See the card on this verse in Jeremiah 23.

sections.h: Judeans in Egypt before the fall
sections.b: Jeremiah 24:8 names "those who live in the land of Egypt" among the bad figs. Zedekiah leaned on Egypt (37:5-7), and some Judeans had already gone there before 586 BC (26:20-23). After the fall a larger group followed against Jeremiah's advice (chapters 42-44). In 25:19 Pharaoh and his court are the first foreign rulers to drink the cup.

sections.h: The city called by my name
sections.b: Jeremiah 21:13 pictures Jerusalem as a rock on the plain that thinks no one can come down on it. In 25:29 the LORD says he begins his harm "on the city that is called by my name." The nearer to God, the sooner the judgment: Ezekiel 9:6 and 1 Peter 4:17 say the same.

sections.h: Foreigner, orphan and widow
sections.b: Jeremiah 22:3 repeats the law's three protected groups: the foreigner who lives among you, the orphan and the widow. The royal house is to protect them and to spill no innocent blood in the place.

sections.h: Byword, taunt and curse
sections.b: The curses of Deuteronomy 28 supply the vocabulary of 24:9-10 ("a byword, a taunt and a curse"; the sword, the famine and the disease) and the unburied dead of 25:33.

sections.h: Moab and Abarim in Jeremiah 22 and 25
sections.b: Moab is named with Edom and Ammon in the cup list (25:21). Its mountains of Abarim mark the eastern limit of the cry in 22:20.

sections.h: Edom in the cup list
sections.b: Edom, Moab and the Ammonites are named together at 25:21; they sent envoys to Jerusalem in Zedekiah's reign (27:3). Their own oracles follow at 48-49.

sections.h: Ammon in the cup list
sections.b: The Ammonites drink after Edom and Moab (25:21). Their own oracle is Jeremiah 49:1-6.

sections.h: Tyre and Sidon in the cup list
sections.b: All the kings of Tyre and Sidon and of the coastland across the sea drink the cup (25:22). Isaiah 23:15 gives Tyre its own seventy years.

sections.h: The Philistine cities in the cup list
sections.b: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and what is left of Ashdod drink (25:20). Gath is not named. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in 604 BC.

sections.h: Elam and Media in the cup list
sections.b: Elam and Media are the farthest east on the list (25:25). In the Greek, Elam and the Persians stand there. The Medes later join Cyrus against Babylon (51:11, 28).

sections.h: Unburied in Jeremiah 22 and 25
sections.b: Jehoiakim is to be buried like a donkey, dragged off and thrown beyond the gates (22:19). The slain of the day of the LORD will lie unmourned and unburied, like manure (25:33).
